```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Crash data often hold several counts for each site: crashes of each
severity, or of each type. `countreg_mv()` fits one count regression for
each outcome in one model. Each outcome has its own family, mean formula
and distribution-parameter formulas.

This is the direct way to model counts by category. A total and its split
across categories is the other way; see
`vignette("total-allocation-models")`.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
w <- washington_roads
w$pdo <- w$Total_crashes - w$Injury_crashes
w$injury <- w$Injury_crashes
colSums(w[, c("pdo", "injury")])
```

## 1. One family for each outcome

Outcomes can behave differently. Property damage only (PDO) crashes are
frequent; injury crashes are rarer and can be more skewed. So each
outcome can have its own family:

```{r fit}
m <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                 data = w, family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"))
summary(m)
```

The coefficients are named `<outcome>:<term>`. `family` takes one code for
every outcome, or one per outcome. Different right-hand sides are given as
a list of formulas, one per outcome:

```{r formulas}
m2 <- countreg_mv(list(pdo = pdo ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                       injury = injury ~ lnaadt + offset(lnlength)),
                  data = w, family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"))
AIC(m, m2)
```

`dis_param_formula_1` and `dis_param_formula_2` take one formula for every
outcome or a list named by outcome, so the dispersion of one outcome can
depend on covariates while the others stay constant.

## 2. Choosing the families

The equations are fitted together, but in this version they are
independent given the covariates: the log-likelihood is the sum of the
equations' log-likelihoods, and each equation's estimates equal those of a
separate `countreg()` fit. So the family of each outcome can be chosen by
comparing fits that change only that outcome's family:

```{r families}
fams <- list(c("NB2", "NB2"), c("NB2", "PIG"), c("NB2", "PLN"),
             c("PIG", "PIG"))
sapply(fams, function(f) {
  fit <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 +
                       offset(lnlength), data = w, family = f)
  c(pdo = f[1], injury = f[2], AIC = round(AIC(fit), 1))
})
```

Here the choices fit almost equally well (the AICs are within 0.3), so
the simpler NB2 is a reasonable choice for both outcomes. With rarer or
more skewed outcomes the differences between families are larger.

## 3. Tests across equations

One fit gives the covariance of all the estimates, so hypotheses that
involve several equations can be tested. Is the effect of traffic the
same for PDO and injury crashes?

```{r wald}
b <- coef(m)
V <- vcov(m)
a <- c("pdo:lnaadt", "injury:lnaadt")
diff <- b[a[1]] - b[a[2]]
se <- sqrt(V[a[1], a[1]] + V[a[2], a[2]] - 2 * V[a[1], a[2]])
c(difference = unname(diff), z = unname(diff / se),
  p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(unname(diff / se))))
```

Traffic increases PDO crashes clearly more than injury crashes
(p < 0.001), so the share of injury crashes falls as traffic grows. The
covariance between the two estimates is zero here, because the equations
are independent; with correlated equations it would not be.

## 4. Predictions

`predict()` gives a matrix of expected counts, one column per outcome.
`type = "prob"` gives, for each outcome, the probabilities of the counts
0, 1, 2, ..., and `simulate()` draws all outcomes at once:

```{r predict}
nd <- w[c(1, 50, 200), ]
predict(m, newdata = nd)
lapply(predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 3), round, 3)
```

`tidy()` has an `outcome` column, and `residuals()`, `fitted()`,
`confint()` and `glance()` work as for other models.

## 5. Correlated outcomes

The counts of different severity levels at a site are usually correlated:
unobserved conditions that raise PDO crashes also raise injury crashes.
This version treats the equations as independent given the covariates, so
that correlation is not modeled. Multivariate models with shared random
effects (correlated random parameters across equations) and copula models
are planned.
